answer.answer:
Perhexiline repurposing against fatty-acid oxidation in cytarabine-residual oxidative AML

Hypothesis. In primary human AML in which a cytarabine pulse leaves residual cells with oxidative and fatty-acid-oxidation-associated features, perhexiline will lower long-chain fatty-acid oxidation and reduce survival of that residual population relative to matched normal hematopoietic progenitors. The original indication of perhexiline is angina; that approval status is unverified prior knowledge and requires a regulatory source. The biological context is cytarabine-residual disease in primary blasts and patient-derived xenografts. Bulk viability, ROS-low stem-cell-like fractions, residual oxidative cells, and myeloid differentiation are separate endpoints. Venetoclax with azacitidine is an established AML metabolic regimen and functions here only as a mechanistic comparator [S3].

Supported premises. In the specimens studied, functionally defined leukemia stem cells frequently had low reactive oxygen species and elevated BCL-2, and BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells [S1]. That work supports investigation of a selective metabolic dependency and shows that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor cannot be assumed to have a therapeutic window across AML [S1]. In cytarabine-treated models, residual cells were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells; they showed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features, and altering that state changed treatment response in those settings [S2]. Those findings are model-restricted and do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound [S2]. Patient-associated and experimental observations link venetoclax-azacitidine to leukemia-stem-cell TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects [S3]. Independently, DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and affected disease-related endpoints in the AML models tested [S4].

Speculative bridges. Unverified prior knowledge holds that perhexiline inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase and thereby restricts mitochondrial entry of long-chain fatty acids, with exposure shaped by CYP2D6 genotype and therapeutic drug monitoring. The packet contains no perhexiline data. The first speculative bridge is that the fatty-acid-oxidation-associated residual state [S2] is CPT-dependent at exposures that normal CD34-positive progenitors tolerate. The second is that this dependency is separable from the ROS-low, BCL-2-high state [S1] and from DHODH-linked differentiation [S4]. Both bridges are assumptions. The medium-chain fatty-acid bypass used below is likewise unverified prior knowledge about CPT-1 substrate routing.

Alternative explanations. A signal could arise from nonspecific mitochondrial injury, off-target channel effects, or bulk cytarabine sensitization. Residual cells might share the oxidative-phosphorylation vulnerability already addressed by BCL-2 inhibition [S1][S3]. A lower leukemic burden might reflect differentiation [S4] or enrichment of a slower-cycling subset. The residual oxidative phenotype may be limited to particular models or genotypes and may be absent in primary samples.

Discriminating preclinical test. In paired primary AML and matched normal hematopoietic progenitors, prospectively separate bulk blasts, a ROS-low fraction [S1], and cells persisting after a cytarabine pulse [S2]. Expose each population to perhexiline alone and to perhexiline plus cytarabine, alongside vehicle, venetoclax, and a DHODH inhibitor [S1][S3][S4]. Measure viability, colony formation, oxygen consumption, and 13C-long-chain-fatty-acid labeling of TCA intermediates. Include a medium-chain fatty-acid condition and CPT1A disruption as a genetic phenocopy. Score morphology and myeloid surface markers so a differentiation outcome is measured directly [S4]. Compare each leukemic fraction with normal progenitors at the same concentration, and map concentrations to human plasma levels only after independent pharmacokinetic verification.

Falsifying observation. The claim fails if perhexiline leaves residual-cell fatty-acid oxidation and viability intact at an exposure that inhibits CPT in a positive-control assay; if leukemia suppression persists after the medium-chain bypass and is absent after CPT1A loss; if residual AML cells and normal progenitors are equally sensitive; or if activity is confined to the ROS-low BCL-2-high fraction while the cytarabine-residual population is spared.

Limitations. Nothing in the packet identifies this drug, its label, or a safe exposure. Mitochondrial inhibition is not automatically selective [S1]. Cytarabine-residual metabolism in models is not clinical proof [S2]. Genotype, niche support, and compensatory use of glucose or amino acids could remove an in vitro fatty-acid-oxidation effect. If primary sources confirm historical hepatic or neurologic toxicity, that constraint remains even when the cell-based mechanism is real. Selectivity against normal progenitors, cardiomyocyte oxidative metabolism, and a DHODH-style differentiation readout must be shown directly, because a pathway association alone is not evidence of efficacy.

ranking.item: Perhexiline repurposing against fatty-acid oxidation in cytarabine-residual oxidative AML
